items.stem: Which statement is Newton's first law?
options: An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
An object always moves in the direction of the largest force
items.answer: An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
items.markingKey: First law: no resultant force → no change in velocity.

items.stem: Explain why a passenger in a bus lurches forward when the bus brakes suddenly.
items.answer: The passenger has inertia and tends to continue moving at the original velocity (first law); the brakes act on the bus, not directly on the passenger, until the seat or belt provides a force.
items.markingKey: inertia / first law [1]; no force on passenger initially to decelerate them [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the normal contact force on a book on a table is not the Newton's third law pair of its weight.
items.answer: The two forces act on the same object (the book) and are of different types (contact and gravitational); a third law pair acts on different objects and is the same type.
items.markingKey: same object [1]; different types [1] [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1100 kg accelerates at 1.5 m s⁻². Work out the resultant force on it.
items.markingKey: F = ma = 1100 × 1.5 = 1650 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sledge of mass 40 kg is pulled by a driving force of 24 N against a total resistive force of 8.0 N. Calculate the acceleration.

A sledge of mass 25 kg moving at 0 m s⁻¹ experiences a driving force of 56.3 N and a resistive force of 18.8 N for 8.0 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (b) Calculate the final speed. (c) Calculate the distance travelled in this time.
items.answer: (a) 1.5 m s⁻² (b) 12 m s⁻¹ (c) 48 m
items.markingKey: (a) resultant 37.5 N [1]; a = 1.5 m s⁻² [1] (b) v = u + at = 12 m s⁻¹ [1] (c) s = ut + ½at² = 48 m [1] [4]

items.stem: A car of mass 1500 kg tows a trailer of mass 600 kg along a straight, level road in Karachi. The driving force from the car is 2400 N and the total resistive force on car and trailer is 300 N, shared in proportion to their masses. (a) Calculate the acceleration of the system. (b) State Newton's third law and apply it to the tow bar.
items.answer: (a) 1.0 m s⁻² (b) If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A: the bar pulls the trailer forwards and the trailer pulls the car backwards with equal force.
items.markingKey: (a) a = (2400 − 300)/(1500 + 600) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.0 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2] (b) statement [1]; application [1] [2]

items.stem: A tractor of mass 1800 kg pulls a cart of mass 600 kg on a level track with a driving force of 3000 N. Resistive forces total 300 N and are shared in proportion to mass. (a) State Newton's third law and apply it to the tow bar. (b) Explain why the acceleration is less when the trailer is loaded with more mass. (c) State what happens to the motion if the driving force becomes equal to the resistive force.
items.answer: (a) If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A: the bar pulls the trailer forwards and the trailer pulls the car backwards with equal force. (b) For the same resultant force, a = F/m; a larger total mass gives a smaller acceleration. (c) The resultant force is zero, so the system moves at constant velocity (first law).
items.markingKey: (a) statement [1]; application [1] [2] (b) a = F/m [1]; larger mass [1] [2] (c) The resultant force is zero, so the system moves at constant velocity (first law) [1]

items.stem: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a mass of 3.0 kg. What is the acceleration?
items.answer: 4.0 m s⁻²

items.stem: The property of an object that resists changes to its velocity is its …
items.answer: mass
items.markingKey: Mass is a measure of inertia.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The property of an object that resists changes to its velocity is its … (b) Which unit is equivalent to the newton?
items.answer: (a) mass (b) kg m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) Mass is a measure of inertia. (b) F = ma.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by saying that mass is a measure of an object's resistance to changes in velocity.
items.answer: For a given resultant force, a = F/m, so a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration: the velocity changes less quickly.
items.markingKey: a = F/m [1]; larger mass → smaller acceleration for same force [1] [2]

items.stem: A rocket in deep space with its engine off continues to move. Explain why no force is needed to keep it moving.
items.answer: By Newton's first law a body moves with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts; with no drag or gravity, no force is needed to maintain the velocity.
items.markingKey: first law [1]; force needed only to change velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a rocket engine produces a forward force on the rocket.
items.answer: The engine pushes exhaust gas backwards (giving it momentum); by Newton's third law the gas pushes the rocket forwards with an equal force.
items.markingKey: force on gas backwards [1]; equal and opposite force on rocket (N3) [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the Newton's third law pair force when a magnet attracts an iron nail. Isla says the two forces cancel. Explain why Isla is wrong.
items.answer: The pair force: the nail attracts the magnet with an equal magnetic force. They act on different objects, so they cannot cancel; each affects the motion of the object it acts on.
items.markingKey: pair force described with same type and magnitude [1]; acts on different object [1]; so cannot cancel [1] [3]

items.stem: A rocket sled is driven along a frictionless track by its engine. The resultant force is multiplied by 4 while the mass stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the acceleration changes.
items.answer: The acceleration becomes 4 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using a = F/m: acceleration ∝ resultant force; factor = 4.00 = 4.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates at 1.5 m s⁻². What is the resultant force on it?
A train of mass 60 000 kg accelerates at 1.5 m s⁻². What is the resultant force on it?
A resultant force of 16 000 N acts on a train of mass 40 000 kg. Calculate the acceleration.
items.markingKey: a = F/m = 16 000/40 000 = 0.40 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A resultant force of 960 N acts on a car of mass 1200 kg. Calculate the acceleration.
items.markingKey: a = F/m = 960/1200 = 0.80 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A train of mass 40 000 kg is pulled by a driving force of 96 000 N against a total resistive force of 16 000 N. Calculate the acceleration.
items.answer: 2.0 m s⁻²

items.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg is pulled by a driving force of 2520 N against a total resistive force of 720 N. Calculate the acceleration.
items.answer: 1.5 m s⁻²

items.stem: A tractor of mass 1800 kg pulls a cart of mass 400 kg on a level track with a driving force of 2400 N. Resistive forces total 200 N and are shared in proportion to mass. (a) State Newton's third law and apply it to the tow bar. (b) Explain why the acceleration is less when the trailer is loaded with more mass.
items.answer: (a) If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A: the bar pulls the trailer forwards and the trailer pulls the car backwards with equal force. (b) For the same resultant force, a = F/m; a larger total mass gives a smaller acceleration.
items.markingKey: (a) statement [1]; application [1] [2] (b) a = F/m [1]; larger mass [1] [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1500 kg tows a trailer of mass 600 kg along a straight, level road in Manila. The driving force from the car is 2400 N and the total resistive force on car and trailer is 400 N, shared in proportion to their masses. (a) Calculate the acceleration of the system. (b) Explain why the acceleration is less when the trailer is loaded with more mass. (c) State what happens to the motion if the driving force becomes equal to the resistive force.
items.answer: (a) 0.952 m s⁻² (b) For the same resultant force, a = F/m; a larger total mass gives a smaller acceleration. (c) The resultant force is zero, so the system moves at constant velocity (first law).
items.markingKey: (a) a = (2400 − 400)/(1500 + 600) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.952 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2] (b) a = F/m [1]; larger mass [1] [2] (c) The resultant force is zero, so the system moves at constant velocity (first law) [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct expression for the weight of an object of mass m?
items.answer: mg
items.markingKey: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength.

items.stem: A ball-bearing is released in a tall tube of oil. Describe and explain its motion.
items.answer: It accelerates initially; as speed increases, viscous drag increases, reducing the resultant force and acceleration; when drag + upthrust = weight, it moves at constant terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: initial acceleration [1]; drag increases with speed [1]; terminal velocity when forces balance [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a car reaches a top speed even though the engine still provides a driving force.
items.answer: Air resistance and other resistive forces increase with speed; at top speed they equal the driving force so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.
items.markingKey: resistive forces increase with speed [1]; equal driving force → zero resultant [1] [2]

items.stem: A model parachute of mass 0.080 kg falls through air. The drag force is given by F = kv² where k = 4.9 × 10⁻² kg m⁻¹. Determine the terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: at terminal velocity kv² = mg → v = √(mg/k) = √(0.785/4.9 × 10⁻²) = 4.00 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A golf ball of mass 0.046 kg falls through air. The drag force is given by F = kv² where k = 2.3 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. Calculate its acceleration when its speed is 31.0 m s⁻¹.

A small sphere of mass 0.020 kg is dropped from a tall building in Istanbul. Its terminal velocity in air is 5.0 m s⁻¹, and the drag force is proportional to v². (a) Calculate the acceleration when the speed is 2.5 m s⁻¹. (b) Sketch the acceleration-time graph from release.
items.answer: (a) 7.36 m s⁻² (b) Starts at 9.81 m s⁻² and decreases (curving) towards zero.
items.markingKey: (a) drag = ¼ weight so resultant = ¾mg; a = 0.75g [2] (b) starts at g [1]; decreases to zero [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the weight of a 65 kg astronaut on Earth?
Answer both parts. (a) Which statement about drag force on an object moving through a fluid is correct? (b) Which is the correct expression for the weight of an object of mass m?
items.answer: (a) It increases as the speed of the object increases (b) mg
items.markingKey: (a) Drag depends on speed (often ∝ v²), shape and the fluid. (b) Weight = mass × gravitational field strength.

items.stem: Explain why a skydiver in a head-down position has a higher terminal velocity than one spread out horizontally.
items.answer: A smaller cross-sectional area gives less drag at a given speed, so the speed must be higher before drag equals weight.
items.markingKey: smaller area, less drag [1]; higher speed needed to balance weight [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the weight of an astronaut is less on the Moon although the mass is unchanged.
items.answer: Weight = mg; g on the Moon (about 1.6 N kg⁻¹) is smaller than on Earth, while mass (amount of matter) does not depend on location.
items.markingKey: W = mg with smaller g [1]; mass unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a cyclist free-wheeling down a slope reaches a constant speed.
items.answer: The component of weight down the slope is constant but air resistance increases with speed until it (plus friction) equals that component; then the resultant force is zero.
items.markingKey: weight component constant [1]; drag increases to balance it [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena drags a crate of mass 10 kg with a horizontal rope tension of 80 N against friction of 15 N. Work out the acceleration of the box.
items.answer: 6.5 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a = (80 − 15)/10 = 6.5 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A table-tennis ball of mass 0.0027 kg falls through air. The drag force is given by F = kv² where k = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. Work out the terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: at terminal velocity kv² = mg → v = √(mg/k) = √(0.0265/4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 8.14 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Omar drags a crate of mass 15 kg with a horizontal rope tension of 40 N against friction of 20 N. Calculate the acceleration of the box.
items.markingKey: a = (40 − 20)/15 = 1.33 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tennis ball of mass 0.057 kg falls through air. The drag force is given by F = kv² where k = 8.9 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. (a) Calculate its terminal velocity. (b) Calculate its acceleration when its speed is 15.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Explain why its acceleration decreases as it falls.
items.answer: (a) 25.1 m s⁻¹ (b) 6.28 m s⁻² (c) drag increases with speed, so the resultant force decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) kv² = mg [1]; v = 25.1 m s⁻¹ [1] (b) resultant force = 0.358 N [1]; a = 6.28 m s⁻² [1] (c) drag ∝ v² increases, resultant decreases [1] [5]

items.stem: A small sphere of mass 0.060 kg is dropped from a tall building in Dubai. Its terminal velocity in air is 5.0 m s⁻¹, and the drag force is proportional to v². (a) Calculate the drag force at terminal velocity. (b) Calculate the acceleration when the speed is 2.5 m s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) drag = weight = mg: 0.589 N [1] (b) drag = ¼ weight so resultant = ¾mg; a = 0.75g [2]

items.stem: A model parachute of mass 0.020 kg is released from rest. It reaches a terminal velocity of 5.0 m s⁻¹; drag ∝ v². (a) Determine the constant k in F = kv². (b) Sketch the acceleration-time graph from release.
items.answer: (a) 7.85 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹ (b) Starts at 9.81 m s⁻² and decreases (curving) towards zero.
items.markingKey: (a) k = mg/v² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.85 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) starts at g [1]; decreases to zero [1] [2]

items.stem: A model parachute of mass 0.060 kg is released from rest. It reaches a terminal velocity of 8.0 m s⁻¹; drag ∝ v². (a) Calculate the drag force at terminal velocity. (b) Calculate the acceleration when the speed is 4.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Explain why a heavier object of the same size and shape has a greater terminal velocity.
items.answer: (a) 0.589 N (b) 7.36 m s⁻² (c) It needs a larger drag force to balance its larger weight, which requires a higher speed.
items.markingKey: (a) drag = weight = mg: 0.589 N [1] (b) drag = ¼ weight so resultant = ¾mg; a = 0.75g [2] (c) larger weight to balance [1]; higher speed needed [1] [2]

items.stem: What does a free-body diagram show?
options: All the forces the object exerts on other objects
All the forces acting on one object
The forces acting on all objects in a system
items.answer: All the forces acting on one object
items.markingKey: A free-body diagram isolates one object and shows every force acting on it.

items.stem: Explain why a person in a lift feels heavier as the lift starts to move upwards.
items.answer: The floor must provide a resultant upward force to accelerate the person, so the normal contact force is greater than the weight; the person feels this larger contact force.
items.markingKey: upward acceleration needs resultant upward force [1]; normal force > weight [1] [2]

items.stem: Draw and describe the free-body diagram for a parachutist falling at terminal velocity.
items.answer: Two forces: weight downwards and drag (air resistance) upwards, of equal length.
items.markingKey: weight down and drag up [1]; equal magnitude [1] [2]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 650 kg accelerates upwards at 0.50 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.markingKey: T − mg = ±ma → T = 650(9.81 + 0.50) = 6700 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 500 kg accelerates upwards at 2.0 m s⁻². A passenger of mass 70 kg stands on bathroom scales calibrated in newtons inside the lift. (a) Draw a free-body diagram for the passenger. (b) Calculate the reading on the scales. (c) Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.answer: (a) weight 687 N down, normal force up (b) 827 N (c) 5910 N
items.markingKey: (a) two forces correctly labelled [1] (b) N − mg = ma (with sign) [1]; N = 827 N [1] (c) T = 500(9.81 + 2.0) = 5910 N [1] [4]

items.stem: A passenger of mass 70 kg rides in a lift of mass 800 kg in an office block in Cape Town. The lift accelerates upwards at 1.0 m s⁻², travels at a constant 2.0 m s⁻¹ and then decelerates at 1.0 m s⁻² to rest. (a) Calculate the cable tension while accelerating upwards. (b) Calculate the contact force on the passenger while decelerating.
items.markingKey: (a) T = (M + m)(g + a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9400 N with unit [1] [2] (b) N = m(g − a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 617 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A lift of mass 800 kg accelerates upwards at 1.5 m s⁻². What is the tension in the cable?
Explain why the normal contact force on a box on a slope is less than its weight.
items.answer: The normal force balances only the component of weight perpendicular to the slope, W cos θ, which is less than W.
items.markingKey: balances perpendicular component [1]; W cos θ < W [1] [2]

items.stem: A student draws a free-body diagram for a ball in flight showing a "force of the throw". Explain the error.
items.answer: Once the ball leaves the hand, no force from the throw acts; only weight (and air resistance) act. The ball continues moving because of its inertia.
items.markingKey: no throw force after release [1]; only weight (and drag); motion from inertia [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the free-body diagram for a car accelerating along a level road, identifying every force and comparing their sizes. State the direction of the resultant force.
items.answer: Weight down, normal reactions up (equal to weight), driving force forwards larger than air resistance and friction backwards.
items.markingKey: all forces identified [1]; correct relative sizes [1]; resultant direction consistent with motion [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe the free-body diagram for a parachutist decelerating just after the parachute opens, identifying every force and comparing their sizes. State the direction of the resultant force.
items.answer: Weight down, air resistance up, with air resistance larger than weight.
items.markingKey: all forces identified [1]; correct relative sizes [1]; resultant direction consistent with motion [1] [3]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 1000 kg accelerates upwards at 1.5 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.markingKey: T − mg = ±ma → T = 1000(9.81 + 1.5) = 11 300 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A block of mass 8.0 kg slides down a slope inclined at 20° to the horizontal with negligible friction. Calculate the acceleration of the block down the slope and the normal contact force.
items.markingKey: component down slope mg sin 20° = 26.8 N [1]; resultant ÷ m: a = 3.36 m s⁻² [1]; N = mg cos 20° = 73.7 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A block of mass 12 kg slides down a slope inclined at 15° to the horizontal with negligible friction. Calculate the acceleration of the block down the slope and the normal contact force.
items.markingKey: component down slope mg sin 15° = 30.5 N [1]; resultant ÷ m: a = 2.54 m s⁻² [1]; N = mg cos 15° = 114 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 1000 kg accelerates upwards at 1.5 m s⁻². A passenger of mass 60 kg stands on bathroom scales calibrated in newtons inside the lift. (a) Draw a free-body diagram for the passenger. (b) Calculate the reading on the scales. (c) Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.answer: (a) weight 589 N down, normal force up (b) 679 N (c) 11 300 N
items.markingKey: (a) two forces correctly labelled [1] (b) N − mg = ma (with sign) [1]; N = 679 N [1] (c) T = 1000(9.81 + 1.5) = 11 300 N [1]; comment that scales read more/less than weight [1] [5]

items.stem: In a hotel in Kathmandu, a lift of mass 900 kg carrying a passenger of mass 80 kg speeds up at 0.60 m s⁻², moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹, then slows at 0.60 m s⁻² to stop at the top floor. (a) Calculate the cable tension at constant velocity. (b) Explain why the passenger feels lighter while the lift slows down at the top. (c) Calculate the time taken to reach the constant speed.
items.answer: (a) 9610 N (b) The lift accelerates downwards so the resultant force on the passenger is downwards; the normal force is less than the weight. (c) 5.0 s
items.markingKey: (a) T = (M + m)g: 9610 N [1] (b) acceleration downwards [1]; normal force < weight [1] [2] (c) t = v/a: 5.0 s [1]

items.stem: A passenger of mass 80 kg rides in a lift of mass 900 kg in an office block in Bogotá. (b) Calculate the contact force on the passenger while decelerating.
items.markingKey: (a) T = (M + m)(g + a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 10 200 N with unit [1] [2] (b) N = m(g − a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 737 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: In a hotel in Seoul, a lift of mass 700 kg carrying a passenger of mass 80 kg speeds up at 1.4 m s⁻², moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹, then slows at 1.4 m s⁻² to stop at the top floor. (a) Calculate the cable tension while accelerating upwards. (b) Calculate the cable tension at constant velocity. (c) Calculate the contact force on the passenger while decelerating. (d) Calculate the time taken to reach the constant speed.
items.markingKey: (a) T = (M + m)(g + a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8740 N with unit [1] [2] (b) T = (M + m)g: 7650 N [1] (c) N = m(g − a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 673 N with unit [1] [2] (d) t = v/a: 2.14 s [1]

items.stem: Newton's third law pairs of forces …
options: act on the same object and cancel out
act on different objects and are of the same type
are of different types, such as weight and normal contact force
items.answer: act on different objects and are of the same type
items.markingKey: N3 pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, same type, on different bodies.

items.markingKey: a = F/m = 0.40/0.80 = 0.50 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.markingKey: F = ma = 40 × 1.5 = 60 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A resultant force of 150 N acts on a cyclist and bicycle of mass 75 kg. Work out the acceleration.
items.answer: 2.0 m s⁻²

items.stem: A tractor of mass 1200 kg pulls a cart of mass 800 kg on a level track with a driving force of 2400 N. Resistive forces total 200 N and are shared in proportion to mass. (a) Calculate the acceleration of the system. (b) State Newton's third law and apply it to the tow bar.

items.markingKey: (a) for trailer: T − 57.1 = 600 × 1.05 (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 686 N with unit [1] [3] (b) The resultant force is zero, so the system moves at constant velocity (first law) [1]

items.stem: Which statement about drag force on an object moving through a fluid is correct?
options: It increases as the speed of the object increases
It acts in the direction of motion
items.answer: It increases as the speed of the object increases
items.markingKey: Drag depends on speed (often ∝ v²), shape and the fluid.

items.stem: A rover of mass 70 kg is weighed on Earth and then on the Moon, where g = 1.62 N kg⁻¹. State its mass and weight in each place and explain the difference.
items.answer: Mass 70 kg in both places; weight 687 N on Earth and 113 N on the Moon. Mass is the quantity of matter; weight = mg depends on the local field strength.
items.markingKey: mass unchanged [1]; both weights correct [1]; explanation W = mg depends on g [1] [3]

items.stem: A shuttlecock of mass 0.0050 kg falls through air. The drag force is given by F = kv² where k = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. Calculate the terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: at terminal velocity kv² = mg → v = √(mg/k) = √(0.0491/8.1 × 10⁻⁴) = 7.78 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Hana drags a crate of mass 5.0 kg with a horizontal rope tension of 30 N against friction of 12 N. The box starts from rest and the push lasts 4.0 s, after which only friction acts. Calculate the maximum speed and the further distance travelled before the box stops.

A model parachute of mass 0.060 kg is released from rest. It reaches a terminal velocity of 5.0 m s⁻¹; drag ∝ v². (a) Calculate the drag force at terminal velocity. (b) Determine the constant k in F = kv². (c) Explain why a heavier object of the same size and shape has a greater terminal velocity.
items.answer: (a) 0.589 N (b) 2.35 × 10⁻² kg m⁻¹ (c) It needs a larger drag force to balance its larger weight, which requires a higher speed.
items.markingKey: (a) drag = weight = mg: 0.589 N [1] (b) k = mg/v² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.35 × 10⁻² kg m⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) larger weight to balance [1]; higher speed needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Forces of 20 N to the right and 35 N to the left act on a block. What is the resultant force? (b) State the condition for an object to be moving at constant velocity.
items.answer: (a) 15 N to the left (b) The resultant force on it is zero.
items.markingKey: (a) Resultant = 35 − 20 = 15 N towards the larger force. (b) resultant force zero [1]

items.stem: Describe the free-body diagram for a hot-air balloon rising at constant velocity, identifying every force and comparing their sizes. State the direction of the resultant force.
items.answer: Weight down, upthrust up, air resistance down; upthrust = weight + drag.
items.markingKey: all forces identified [1]; correct relative sizes [1]; resultant direction consistent with motion [1] [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Draw and describe the free-body diagram for a parachutist falling at terminal velocity. (b) Explain why the normal contact force on a box on a slope is less than its weight.
items.answer: (a) Two forces: weight downwards and drag (air resistance) upwards, of equal length. (b) The normal force balances only the component of weight perpendicular to the slope, W cos θ, which is less than W.
items.markingKey: (a) weight down and drag up [1]; equal magnitude [1] [2] (b) balances perpendicular component [1]; W cos θ < W [1] [2]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 500 kg accelerates upwards at 0.50 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.markingKey: T − mg = ±ma → T = 500(9.81 + 0.50) = 5160 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 500 kg accelerates downwards at 0.80 m s⁻². A passenger of mass 70 kg stands on bathroom scales calibrated in newtons inside the lift. (a) Draw a free-body diagram for the passenger. (b) Calculate the reading on the scales. (c) Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.answer: (a) weight 687 N down, normal force up (b) 631 N (c) 4510 N
items.markingKey: (a) two forces correctly labelled [1] (b) N − mg = ma (with sign) [1]; N = 631 N [1] (c) T = 500(9.81 − 0.80) = 4510 N [1] [4]

items.stem: A passenger of mass 60 kg rides in a lift of mass 900 kg in an office block in Jakarta. The lift accelerates upwards at 0.60 m s⁻², travels at a constant 2.0 m s⁻¹ and then decelerates at 0.60 m s⁻² to rest. (a) Calculate the cable tension while accelerating upwards. (b) Calculate the cable tension at constant velocity. (c) Explain why the passenger feels lighter while the lift slows down at the top. (d) Calculate the time taken to reach the constant speed.
items.answer: (a) 9990 N (b) 9420 N (c) The lift accelerates downwards so the resultant force on the passenger is downwards; the normal force is less than the weight. (d) 3.33 s
items.markingKey: (a) T = (M + m)(g + a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9990 N with unit [1] [2] (b) T = (M + m)g: 9420 N [1] (c) acceleration downwards [1]; normal force < weight [1] [2] (d) t = v/a: 3.33 s [1]

items.stem: A book rests on a table. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with the weight of the book?
options: The gravitational pull of the book on the Earth
The normal contact force of the table on the book
items.answer: The gravitational pull of the book on the Earth
items.markingKey: Weight is the Earth pulling the book; its pair is the book pulling the Earth (both gravitational).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how a rocket engine produces a forward force on the rocket. (b) A rocket in deep space with its engine off continues to move. Explain why no force is needed to keep it moving.
items.answer: (a) The engine pushes exhaust gas backwards (giving it momentum); by Newton's third law the gas pushes the rocket forwards with an equal force. (b) By Newton's first law a body moves with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts; with no drag or gravity, no force is needed to maintain the velocity.
items.markingKey: (a) force on gas backwards [1]; equal and opposite force on rocket (N3) [1] [2] (b) first law [1]; force needed only to change velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: A rocket sled is driven along a frictionless track by its engine. The mass is increased by 50% while the resultant force stays the same. State and explain how the acceleration changes.
items.answer: The acceleration falls to two thirds.
items.markingKey: Using a = F/m: acceleration ∝ mass^-1.00; factor = 1.50^-1.00 = 0.667. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A resultant force of 37.5 N acts on a sledge of mass 25 kg. Calculate the acceleration.
items.answer: 1.5 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a = F/m = 37.5/25 = 1.5 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A resultant force of 1.50 × 10⁵ N acts on a train of mass 60 000 kg. Calculate the acceleration.
items.answer: 2.5 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a = F/m = 1.50 × 10⁵/60 000 = 2.5 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A resultant force of 1.20 N gives a trolley an acceleration of 1.5 m s⁻². Calculate the mass.
items.markingKey: m = F/a = 1.20/1.5 = 0.80 kg. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tractor of mass 1800 kg pulls a cart of mass 400 kg on a level track with a driving force of 3600 N. Resistive forces total 400 N and are shared in proportion to mass. (a) Calculate the acceleration of the system. (b) Explain why the acceleration is less when the trailer is loaded with more mass.
items.answer: (a) 1.45 m s⁻² (b) For the same resultant force, a = F/m; a larger total mass gives a smaller acceleration.
items.markingKey: (a) a = (3600 − 400)/(1800 + 400) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.45 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2] (b) a = F/m [1]; larger mass [1] [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg tows a trailer of mass 600 kg along a straight, level road in Seoul. The driving force from the car is 4200 N and the total resistive force on car and trailer is 300 N, shared in proportion to their masses. (a) Calculate the acceleration of the system. (b) Explain why the acceleration is less when the trailer is loaded with more mass.
items.answer: (a) 2.17 m s⁻² (b) For the same resultant force, a = F/m; a larger total mass gives a smaller acceleration.
items.markingKey: (a) a = (4200 − 300)/(1200 + 600) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.17 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2] (b) a = F/m [1]; larger mass [1] [2]

items.stem: At terminal velocity, the resultant force on a falling object is …
items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: Drag (plus upthrust) equals weight, so acceleration is zero.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a car reaches a top speed even though the engine still provides a driving force. (b) Explain why the weight of an astronaut is less on the Moon although the mass is unchanged.
items.answer: (a) Air resistance and other resistive forces increase with speed; at top speed they equal the driving force so the resultant force and acceleration are zero. (b) Weight = mg; g on the Moon (about 1.6 N kg⁻¹) is smaller than on Earth, while mass (amount of matter) does not depend on location.
items.markingKey: (a) resistive forces increase with speed [1]; equal driving force → zero resultant [1] [2] (b) W = mg with smaller g [1]; mass unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: A rover of mass 50 kg is weighed on Earth and then on the Moon, where g = 1.62 N kg⁻¹. State its mass and weight in each place and explain the difference.
items.answer: Mass 50 kg in both places; weight 491 N on Earth and 81 N on the Moon. Mass is the quantity of matter; weight = mg depends on the local field strength.
items.markingKey: mass unchanged [1]; both weights correct [1]; explanation W = mg depends on g [1] [3]

items.stem: A box of mass 5.0 kg is pushed across a warehouse floor with a horizontal force of 60 N. The friction force is 25 N. Work out the acceleration of the box.
items.answer: 7.0 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a = (60 − 25)/5.0 = 7.0 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A box of mass 5.0 kg is pushed across a warehouse floor with a horizontal force of 60 N. The friction force is 12 N. The box starts from rest and the push lasts 4.0 s, after which only friction acts. Calculate the maximum speed and the further distance travelled before the box stops.

A small sphere of mass 0.020 kg is dropped from a tall building in Mumbai. Its terminal velocity in air is 6.0 m s⁻¹, and the drag force is proportional to v². (a) Calculate the drag force at terminal velocity. (b) Sketch the acceleration-time graph from release. (c) Explain why a heavier object of the same size and shape has a greater terminal velocity.
items.answer: (a) 0.196 N (b) Starts at 9.81 m s⁻² and decreases (curving) towards zero. (c) It needs a larger drag force to balance its larger weight, which requires a higher speed.
items.markingKey: (a) drag = weight = mg: 0.196 N [1] (b) starts at g [1]; decreases to zero [1] [2] (c) larger weight to balance [1]; higher speed needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A lift of mass 800 kg accelerates upwards at 1.5 m s⁻². What is the tension in the cable? (b) Forces of 20 N to the right and 35 N to the left act on a block. What is the resultant force?
items.answer: (a) 9050 N (b) 15 N to the left
items.markingKey: (a) T − mg = ma: T = 800(9.81 + 1.5) = 9050 N. (b) Resultant = 35 − 20 = 15 N towards the larger force.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student draws a free-body diagram for a ball in flight showing a "force of the throw". Explain the error. (b) Explain why the normal contact force on a box on a slope is less than its weight.
items.answer: (a) Once the ball leaves the hand, no force from the throw acts; only weight (and air resistance) act. The ball continues moving because of its inertia. (b) The normal force balances only the component of weight perpendicular to the slope, W cos θ, which is less than W.
items.markingKey: (a) no throw force after release [1]; only weight (and drag); motion from inertia [1] [2] (b) balances perpendicular component [1]; W cos θ < W [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student draws a free-body diagram for a ball in flight showing a "force of the throw". Explain the error. (b) Explain why a person in a lift feels heavier as the lift starts to move upwards.
items.answer: (a) Once the ball leaves the hand, no force from the throw acts; only weight (and air resistance) act. The ball continues moving because of its inertia. (b) The floor must provide a resultant upward force to accelerate the person, so the normal contact force is greater than the weight; the person feels this larger contact force.
items.markingKey: (a) no throw force after release [1]; only weight (and drag); motion from inertia [1] [2] (b) upward acceleration needs resultant upward force [1]; normal force > weight [1] [2]

items.stem: A lift of total mass 1000 kg accelerates downwards at 1.0 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the cable.
items.markingKey: T − mg = ±ma → T = 1000(9.81 − 1.0) = 8810 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]
